solution:
**Least count** is the smallest quantity that a measuring instrument can measure — that is, the value of one smallest division on its scale.

The chapter introduces it while discussing accuracy: "Accuracy depends upon the sensitivity or least count (the smallest quantity that can be measured) of the measuring equipment."

Its significance is that the least count fixes how many significant figures a reading may carry. A burette graduated in 0.1 mL has a least count of 0.1 mL, so a reading is written as 10.2 mL, the last digit being the uncertain one, and the true value is taken to lie between 10.1 mL and 10.3 mL — written \(10.2 \pm 0.1\ \mathrm{mL}\). In general, an instrument of smaller least count gives more significant figures and a more accurate measurement than one of larger least count.

**Significant figures** in a measurement or result are the number of digits known with certainty plus one uncertain (estimated) digit. They express the uncertainty of a measured value: for a burette reading \(10.2 \pm 0.1\ \mathrm{mL}\) the digits 1 and 0 are certain and the last digit 2 is uncertain, so the reading has three significant figures.

**Rules for deciding significant figures** (section 2.3.4):

1. All non-zero digits are significant. e.g. 127.34 g contains five significant figures, which are 1, 2, 7, 3 and 4.

2. All zeros between two non-zero digits are significant. e.g. 120.007 m contains six significant figures.

3. Zeroes on the left of the first non-zero digit are not significant; such a zero only indicates the position of the decimal point. e.g. 0.025 has two significant figures and 0.005 has one.

4. Zeroes at the end of a number are significant if they are on the right side of the decimal point; terminal zeros are not significant if there is no decimal point. e.g. 0.400 g has three significant figures, while 400 g has one. The zeros after the decimal point indicate the least count of the weighing machine: \(400\ \mathrm{g}\), \(4.0 \times 10^2\ \mathrm{g}\) and \(4.00 \times 10^2\ \mathrm{g}\) correspond to least counts of 1 g, 0.1 g and 0.01 g respectively.

5. In numbers written in scientific notation, all digits of the coefficient are significant. e.g. \(2.035 \times 10^2\) has four significant figures and \(3.25 \times 10^{-5}\) has three.

| | Accuracy | Precision |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | Nearness of the measured value to the true (accepted) value | Closeness of several repeated measurements of the same quantity to one another |
| Compared against | The true value, which must be known independently | The other readings of the same set; the true value is not needed |
| Expressed as | Absolute error \(=\) Observed value \(-\) True value, and relative error \(= \dfrac{\text{Absolute error}}{\text{True value}} \times 100\%\) | Absolute deviation \(= |\,\text{Observed value} - \text{Mean}\,|\), and relative deviation \(= \dfrac{\text{Mean absolute deviation}}{\text{Mean}} \times 100\%\) |
| Depends on | The sensitivity or least count of the instrument | The reproducibility of the readings |

The two are not independent: as the chapter puts it, **high precision is a prerequisite for high accuracy**. Readings can be precise (tightly grouped) and still inaccurate if the instrument carries a bias, but readings that scatter widely cannot be relied on to be accurate.

**Percentage composition** is the mass of each constituent element expressed as a percentage of the total mass of the compound. It is found by quantitative determination of the constituent elements; if the percentages do not add up to 100, the difference is taken as the percent oxygen.

**Empirical formula** is the formula giving the *simplest whole-number ratio* of the atoms of the constituent elements in a molecule. It is obtained from the percentage composition: take 100 g of the compound, convert each element's mass to moles by dividing by its atomic mass, divide all the mole values by the smallest of them, and (if the ratios are not whole numbers) multiply throughout by a suitable coefficient.

**Molecular formula** is the formula indicating the *actual* number of atoms of each constituent element in one molecule. It is obtained from the empirical formula once the molar mass is known:

\(r = \dfrac{\text{Molar mass}}{\text{Empirical formula mass}}\), and Molecular formula \(= r \times\) Empirical formula.

For example, a compound with 4.07 % H, 24.27 % C and 71.65 % Cl has the empirical formula \(\mathrm{CH_2Cl}\) (empirical formula mass 49.48); with a molar mass of 98.96 g, \(r = 2\) and the molecular formula is \(\mathrm{C_2H_4Cl_2}\).

In practice the reactants of a reaction are not usually mixed in exactly the proportions the balanced equation demands — a large excess of one reactant is often supplied so that the more expensive reactant is completely converted into the product. The reactant present in the lesser (stoichiometric) amount is consumed first, and once it is gone no further reaction takes place however much of the other reactant remains.

**The reactant that gets consumed first, and thereby limits the amount of product formed, is called the limiting reagent**; the one left over is the excess reagent.

The way to identify it is to calculate, from *each* reactant separately, how much product it could yield if it reacted completely; the limiting reagent is the one that yields the **smaller** amount of product.

Example from the chapter: for \(2\,\mathrm{NO(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{NO_2(g)}\), starting with 8 mol NO and 7 mol \(\mathrm{O_2}\), the NO could give \(8 \times \tfrac{2}{2} = 8\) mol \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) while the \(\mathrm{O_2}\) could give \(7 \times \tfrac{2}{1} = 14\) mol. Because 8 mol is the smaller amount, NO is the limiting reagent and \(\mathrm{O_2}\) is in excess.

**SI units** are the units of the *Système International d'Unités* — the single system of units agreed internationally so that a measurement reported anywhere means the same thing everywhere. It is built on seven base units, one for each base physical quantity: the metre (m) for length, the **kilogram (kg) for mass**, the second (s) for time, the kelvin (K) for temperature, the ampere (A) for electric current, the mole (mol) for amount of substance and the candela (cd) for luminous intensity. Every other unit (the \(\mathrm{m^3}\) for volume, the \(\mathrm{g\ mL^{-1}}\) for density, and so on) is derived from these.

**The SI unit of mass is the kilogram (kg).** It is the one base unit whose name already carries a prefix — the gram is a submultiple of it, not the other way round.

A note on sourcing: This chapter does not itself define the SI system — the phrase "SI unit" appears in it only inside these exercise questions. The system of units is introduced in Chapter 1, *Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry*; what this chapter supplies is the reason units matter here, namely that quantitative analysis "involves measurement of quantities such as mass and volume, by means of some equipment/apparatus such as weighing machine, burette."

All three express the concentration of a solution, i.e. the amount of substance present in a given amount of solution.

**(a) Mole fraction** is the ratio of the number of moles of one component of a solution to the total number of moles of the solution. If a substance A dissolves in a substance B and their numbers of moles are \(n_A\) and \(n_B\), then

Mole fraction of A \(= \dfrac{n_A}{n_A + n_B}\) and mole fraction of B \(= \dfrac{n_B}{n_A + n_B}\).

It is a pure ratio and so has no unit; the mole fractions of all the components of a solution add up to 1.

**(b) Molarity (M)** is the number of moles of the *solute* present in **1 litre of solution**:

Molarity \(= \dfrac{\text{No. of moles of solute}}{\text{Volume of solution in litres}}\), unit \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\).

It is the most widely used unit of concentration. Because it is defined per unit VOLUME, it changes with temperature.

**(c) Molality (m)** is the number of moles of the solute present in **1 kg of solvent**:

Molality \(= \dfrac{\text{No. of moles of solute}}{\text{Mass of solvent in kg}}\), unit \(\mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\).

Because it is defined per unit MASS, and mass is unaffected by temperature, molality does not change with temperature.

**Stoichiometry** is the study of the quantitative relationships between the amounts of reactants consumed and products formed in a chemical reaction, as fixed by the balanced chemical equation. Calculations based on a balanced chemical equation are accordingly called **stoichiometric calculations**.

A balanced equation supplies three kinds of information on which such calculations rest:

i. the number of moles of the reactants involved and of the products formed;

ii. the relative masses of the reactants and products linked with the chemical change; and

iii. the relationship between the volumes of the gaseous reactants and products, at STP.

Because a calculated result must not claim more accuracy than the measurements it was made from. The chapter's rule is that "the accuracy of the final result is limited to the accuracy of the least accurate measurement" — the final result cannot be more accurate than the least accurate number involved in the calculation.

When measured quantities are multiplied, divided, added or subtracted, the arithmetic routinely throws up far more digits than the data justify: dividing 24.27 by 12.01 gives 2.020815..., but neither measurement was known to that many figures. Those extra digits are **not significant** — they carry no information about the quantity, and leaving them in would falsely suggest the result is known more precisely than it is.

Rounding off therefore trims the result back to the number of significant figures the data support, so that the reported value honestly reflects the uncertainty of the measurement. The rules used are: if the digit following the last digit to be kept is less than five, the last digit is left unchanged (46.32 to two significant figures is 46); if it is five or more, the last digit kept is increased by one (52.87 to three significant figures is 52.9).

Because molarity is defined per unit **volume** of solution, and the volume of a solution is temperature dependent.

Molarity \(= \dfrac{\text{No. of moles of solute}}{\text{Volume of solution in litres}}\).

Heating a solution makes it expand, so the same number of moles of solute is now spread through a larger volume and the molarity **falls**; cooling contracts the solution and the molarity **rises**. The numerator does not change, because the amount of solute dissolved is fixed; only the denominator moves.

Contrast molality, \(\dfrac{\text{No. of moles of solute}}{\text{Mass of solvent in kg}}\), which the chapter notes "does not change with temperature since mass remains unaffected with temperature". This is exactly why molality is preferred whenever measurements are to be made over a range of temperatures.

**Analytical chemistry** is the branch of chemistry which deals with the study of separation, identification, and qualitative and quantitative determination of the compositions of different substances. It uses instruments and methods to separate, identify and quantify the matter under study, and so provides chemical or physical information about a sample. It consists of classical, wet chemical methods and modern instrumental methods.

**Why accurate measurement is crucial in science.** Analytical results are not read for their own sake — they are acted on, and a wrong number leads to a wrong decision. The chapter's own list of applications makes the point: chemical analysis monitors the composition of raw materials, intermediates and finished products, and the composition of the air in streets and around industrial plants; in agriculture it determines the composition of soils and fertilizers; in medicine, the composition of medicinal preparations; and it is applied in forensic science, engineering and industry.

Beyond the consequences, accuracy governs what a result may legitimately claim. Every measurement carries an uncertainty set by the least count of the instrument, so a reported value is only meaningful together with the number of significant figures it carries and the error attached to it: "an anlytical chemist has to know how to report the quantitative analytical data, indicating the extent of the accuracy of measurement, perform the mathematical operation and properly express the quatitative error in the result." A measurement quoted without regard to its accuracy overstates what is known, and a conclusion drawn from it is not reproducible by anyone else — which is what makes accurate measurement, and the honest reporting of its uncertainty, the foundation of the whole subject.

Applying the rules of section 2.3.4 — non-zero digits count; zeros between non-zero digits count; leading zeros never count; terminal zeros count only when a decimal point is present; and in scientific notation every digit of the coefficient counts.

**a. 45.26 ft — 4** (all four digits are non-zero, rule 1).

**b. 0.109 in — 3** (the leading zero does not count by rule 3; the zero between 1 and 9 does, by rule 2).

**c. 0.00025 kg — 2** (all four leading zeros only fix the decimal point, rule 3; only 2 and 5 count).

**d. \(2.3659 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}\) — 5** (rule 5: every digit of the coefficient 2.3659 counts; the exponent contributes none).

**e. \(52.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}\) — 3** (the terminal zero lies to the right of the decimal point, so it counts by rule 4).

**f. 0.00020 kg — 2** (leading zeros do not count, but the terminal zero after the decimal point does — so 2 and the final 0).

**g. \(8.50 \times 10^4\ \mathrm{mm}\) — 3** (rule 5 again: 8, 5 and 0 in the coefficient).

**h. 300.0 cg — 4** (the decimal point is present, so all the zeros are significant by rule 4; had it been written 300 cg it would have had only one).

Rounding rule: if the digit following the last digit to be kept is less than five, leave the last digit unchanged; if it is five or more, increase the last digit kept by one.

**a. 25.55 mL \(\to\) 26 mL.** Two significant figures means keeping 2 and 5; the next digit is 5, so the 5 is raised to 6.

**b. 0.00254 m \(\to\) 0.0025 m** (i.e. \(2.5 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}\)). The leading zeros are not significant, so the two significant digits are 2 and 5; the next digit is 4, which is less than 5, so 5 is left unchanged.

**c. \(1.491 \times 10^5\ \mathrm{mg} \to 1.5 \times 10^5\ \mathrm{mg}\).** Keeping 1 and 4, the next digit is 9, so 4 is raised to 5.

**d. 199 g \(\to 2.0 \times 10^2\ \mathrm{g}\).** Keeping 1 and 9, the next digit is 9, so 9 becomes 10 and carries: \(199 \to 200\). Written as "200 g" the terminal zeros would not be significant (rule 4) and the value would read as one significant figure, so the answer must be written in scientific notation as \(2.0 \times 10^2\ \mathrm{g}\) to show that two figures are intended.

**a. \(1.43\ \mathrm{cm^3}\)** — already three significant figures; no rounding needed.

**b. \(458 \times 10^2\ \mathrm{cm}\)** — the coefficient 458 already carries exactly three significant figures; unchanged, better written as \(4.58 \times 10^4\ \mathrm{cm}\).

**c. \(643\ \mathrm{cm^2}\)** — already three; unchanged.

**d. 0.039 m** — this value carries only **two** significant figures (3 and 9; the leading zeros are not significant). It cannot be rounded *to* three, because rounding can only remove figures, never create them: writing 0.0390 m would falsely claim a digit that was never measured. It stays 0.039 m.

**e. \(6.398 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{km} \to 6.40 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{km}\).** Keeping 6, 3 and 9, the next digit is 8, so 9 becomes 10 and carries into the 3. The terminal zero must be written — it is significant.

**f. 0.0179 g** — already three significant figures; unchanged.

**g. 79,000 m** — as written this has only **two** significant figures (terminal zeros with no decimal point, rule 4), so as in (d) it cannot be raised to three. It stays 79,000 m, i.e. \(7.9 \times 10^4\ \mathrm{m}\).

**h. \(42{,}150 \to 4.22 \times 10^4\)** (42,200). Keeping 4, 2 and 1, the next digit is 5, so 1 is raised to 2.

**i. \(649.85 \to 650.\)**, i.e. \(6.50 \times 10^2\). Keeping 6, 4 and 9, the next digit is 8, so 9 becomes 10 and carries into the 4. Scientific notation is needed to show that the terminal zero is significant.

**j. \(23{,}642{,}000\ \mathrm{mm} \to 2.36 \times 10^7\ \mathrm{mm}\).** Keeping 2, 3 and 6, the next digit is 4, which is less than 5, so 6 is left unchanged.

**k. \(0.0041962\ \mathrm{kg} \to 0.00420\ \mathrm{kg}\)**, i.e. \(4.20 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg}\). The significant digits are 4, 1, 9, 6, 2; keeping the first three, the next digit is 6, so 9 becomes 10 and carries into the 1.

In addition and subtraction the result is limited by the term known to the *coarsest place value*, not by the term with fewest significant figures.

**a.** Write every term with the common exponent \(10^3\):

\(2.3 \times 10^3 + 42.2 \times 10^3 + 9.04 \times 10^3 + 871 \times 10^3\)

\(= (2.3 + 42.2 + 9.04 + 871) \times 10^3 = 924.54 \times 10^3\ \mathrm{mL}\)

Of the four terms, \(8.71 \times 10^5\) is the coarsest: its last significant digit sits in the \(10^3\) place, whereas the others are known to \(10^2\) or \(10^1\). The sum must therefore be rounded to the nearest \(10^3\):

\(924.54 \times 10^3 \to 925 \times 10^3 = \mathbf{9.25 \times 10^5\ mL}\)

**b.** \(319.5 - 20460 - 0.0639 - 45.642 - 4.173\)

\(= -20190.3789\ \mathrm{g}\)

Here 20460 g is the coarsest term: it carries no decimal places at all, and by rule 4 its terminal zero is not significant, so it is known only to the nearest 10 g. Rounding the sum to four significant figures gives

\(\mathbf{-2.019 \times 10^4\ g}\) (that is, \(-20190\ \mathrm{g}\)).

The negative sign is real: the three quantities being subtracted from 319.5 g total far more than 319.5 g.

Exponential (scientific) notation writes a number as \(N \times 10^n\), where \(1 \leqslant N < 10\) and \(n\) is the number of places the decimal point has been moved — negative when it is moved to the right, positive when moved to the left. Every digit of \(N\) is retained, so the number of significant figures is unchanged.

**a. \(0.0003498 = 3.498 \times 10^{-4}\)** (decimal moved 4 places to the right).

**b. \(235.4678 = 2.354678 \times 10^{2}\)** (decimal moved 2 places to the left).

**c. \(70000.0 = 7.00000 \times 10^{4}\)** (decimal moved 4 places to the left). The zeros must all be kept: the printed decimal point makes them significant, so this value carries six significant figures.

**d. \(1569.00 = 1.56900 \times 10^{3}\)** (decimal moved 3 places to the left). Again the two terminal zeros are significant and must be retained, giving six significant figures.

**a. \(1.230 \times 10^4\) — 4 significant figures.** By rule 5 all the digits of the coefficient count, and the terminal zero counts because it stands to the right of the decimal point: 1, 2, 3, 0.

**b. 0.002030 — 4 significant figures.** The three leading zeros are not significant (rule 3); the zero between 2 and 3 is (rule 2); and the terminal zero after the decimal point is (rule 4). The significant digits are 2, 0, 3, 0.

**c. \(1.23 \times 10^4\) — 3 significant figures** (1, 2, 3). Note that this is the same magnitude as (a) but one figure less precise, the difference being exactly the written terminal zero.

**d. \(1.89 \times 10^{-4}\) — 3 significant figures** (1, 8, 9). The exponent \(-4\) contributes none; it only fixes the position of the decimal point.

Each quantity is rewritten in the other form — exponential quantities as ordinary decimals and the ordinary decimal as an exponential — keeping every significant figure so the precision is unchanged.

**a. \(1.230 \times 10^4 = 12300\)** — the decimal point moves 4 places to the right. Written this way the value looks like three significant figures, so \(1.230 \times 10^4\) is the honest form; the exponential notation is what preserves the significant terminal zero.

**b. \(0.002030 = 2.030 \times 10^{-3}\)** — the decimal point moves 3 places to the right, so the exponent is \(-3\); the terminal zero is retained, keeping four significant figures.

**c. \(1.23 \times 10^4 = 12300\)** — the same decimal digits as (a), but only three significant figures were ever claimed.

**d. \(1.89 \times 10^{-4} = 0.000189\)** — the decimal point moves 4 places to the left.

The molar mass is the sum of the atomic masses of all the atoms in the formula unit, the water of crystallisation included.

**a. Copper sulphate crystal, \(\mathrm{CuSO_4 \cdot 5H_2O}\)**

\(= 63.5 + 32 + (4 \times 16) + 5(2 \times 1 + 16)\)

\(= 63.5 + 32 + 64 + 5 \times 18 = 63.5 + 32 + 64 + 90\)

\(= \mathbf{249.5\ g\ mol^{-1}}\)

**b. Sodium carbonate decahydrate, \(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3 \cdot 10H_2O}\)**

\(= (2 \times 23) + 12 + (3 \times 16) + 10 \times 18\)

\(= 46 + 12 + 48 + 180\)

\(= \mathbf{286\ g\ mol^{-1}}\)

**c. Mohr's salt, \(\mathrm{FeSO_4(NH_4)_2SO_4 \cdot 6H_2O}\)**

The formula contains one Fe, two sulfate groups, two ammonium groups and six waters:

\(= 56 + [32 + (4 \times 16)] + 2[14 + (4 \times 1)] + [32 + (4 \times 16)] + 6 \times 18\)

\(= 56 + 96 + 36 + 96 + 108\)

\(= \mathbf{392\ g\ mol^{-1}}\)

[Textbook note (not an error): the atomic-mass list printed with this item gives Pb, P, O, K, Cr, Na and N but omits **H**, which part (c) needs — macrocosmic salt \(\mathrm{NaNH_4HPO_4 \cdot 4H_2O}\) contains thirteen hydrogen atoms per formula unit. H = 1 is supplied by the list printed with the item immediately above and is used in the answer.]

Percentage of an element \(= \dfrac{\text{total mass of that element in the formula unit}}{\text{molar mass of the compound}} \times 100\).

**a. Lead phosphate, \(\mathrm{Pb_3(PO_4)_2}\)**

Molar mass \(= (3 \times 207) + 2[31 + (4 \times 16)] = 621 + 190 = 811\)

\(\%\ \mathrm{Pb} = \dfrac{621}{811} \times 100 = 76.57\%\)

\(\%\ \mathrm{P} = \dfrac{62}{811} \times 100 = 7.64\%\)

\(\%\ \mathrm{O} = \dfrac{128}{811} \times 100 = 15.78\%\)  (total 99.99 %)

**b. Potassium dichromate, \(\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}\)**

Molar mass \(= (2 \times 39) + (2 \times 52) + (7 \times 16) = 78 + 104 + 112 = 294\)

\(\%\ \mathrm{K} = \dfrac{78}{294} \times 100 = 26.53\%\)

\(\%\ \mathrm{Cr} = \dfrac{104}{294} \times 100 = 35.37\%\)

\(\%\ \mathrm{O} = \dfrac{112}{294} \times 100 = 38.10\%\)  (total 100.00 %)

**c. Macrocosmic salt, \(\mathrm{NaNH_4HPO_4 \cdot 4H_2O}\)** (taking H = 1, which this item's own list omits but the previous item supplies)

The formula unit holds 1 Na, 1 N, 13 H (4 in \(\mathrm{NH_4}\), 1 acidic, 8 in the four waters), 1 P and 8 O (4 in the phosphate, 4 in the waters).

Molar mass \(= 23 + 14 + 13 + 31 + (8 \times 16) = 23 + 14 + 13 + 31 + 128 = 209\)

\(\%\ \mathrm{Na} = \dfrac{23}{209} \times 100 = 11.00\%\)

\(\%\ \mathrm{N} = \dfrac{14}{209} \times 100 = 6.70\%\)

\(\%\ \mathrm{H} = \dfrac{13}{209} \times 100 = 6.22\%\)

\(\%\ \mathrm{P} = \dfrac{31}{209} \times 100 = 14.83\%\)

\(\%\ \mathrm{O} = \dfrac{128}{209} \times 100 = 61.24\%\)  (total 99.99 %)

Green vitriol is \(\mathrm{FeSO_4 \cdot 7H_2O}\); taking H = 1 as well as the masses given,

Molar mass \(= 56 + 32 + (4 \times 16) + 7 \times 18 = 56 + 32 + 64 + 126 = 278\)

**Percentage composition**

\(\%\ \mathrm{Fe} = \dfrac{56}{278} \times 100 = 20.14\%\)

\(\%\ \mathrm{S} = \dfrac{32}{278} \times 100 = 11.51\%\)

\(\%\ \mathrm{H} = \dfrac{14}{278} \times 100 = 5.04\%\)

\(\%\ \mathrm{O} = \dfrac{64 + 112}{278} \times 100 = \dfrac{176}{278} \times 100 = 63.31\%\)  (total 100.00 %)

**Masses in 4.54 kg of the crystals**

Mass of iron \(= \dfrac{56}{278} \times 4.54 = \mathbf{0.915\ kg}\)

Mass of water of crystallisation \(= \dfrac{126}{278} \times 4.54 = \mathbf{2.058\ kg}\)

(As a check, the water is \(\dfrac{126}{278} \times 100 = 45.32\%\) of the crystals by mass.)

One molecule of haemoglobin contains four atoms of iron, so the mass of iron in one mole of haemoglobin is

\(4 \times 55.84 = 223.36\ \mathrm{g}\)

That mass is 0.335 % of the molecular mass \(M\):

\(\dfrac{223.36}{M} \times 100 = 0.335\)

\(\therefore\ M = \dfrac{223.36 \times 100}{0.335} = \dfrac{22336}{0.335}\)

\(\therefore\ M = \mathbf{66674.6\ g\ mol^{-1}}\)

The method is the standard one for finding a molecular mass from a minor constituent: because the number of atoms of that element per molecule is known, its mass per mole is fixed, and its percentage then fixes the whole.

The percentages add to \(43.4 + 11.3 + 45.3 = 100.0\), so no element is missing and no oxygen has to be found by difference.

Take 100 g of the substance and convert each mass to moles:

Moles of Na \(= \dfrac{43.4}{23} = 1.887\)

Moles of C \(= \dfrac{11.3}{12} = 0.942\)

Moles of O \(= \dfrac{45.3}{16} = 2.831\)

Divide throughout by the smallest value, 0.942:

Na \(= \dfrac{1.887}{0.942} = 2.00\), C \(= \dfrac{0.942}{0.942} = 1\), O \(= \dfrac{2.831}{0.942} = 3.01\)

The simplest whole-number ratio Na : C : O is \(2 : 1 : 3\).

\(\therefore\) the empirical formula is \(\mathbf{Na_2CO_3}\) — sodium carbonate.

The oxide contains 70.0 % of the metal M, so the remaining \(100 - 70.0 = 30.0\%\) is oxygen.

Take 100 g of the oxide: 70.0 g of M and 30.0 g of O.

Moles of M \(= \dfrac{70.0}{56} = 1.25\)

Moles of O \(= \dfrac{30.0}{16} = 1.875\)

Divide by the smaller value, 1.25:

M \(= 1\), O \(= \dfrac{1.875}{1.25} = 1.5\)

The ratio \(1 : 1.5\) is not whole, so multiply both by 2:

M : O \(= 2 : 3\)

\(\therefore\) the empirical formula of the oxide is \(\mathbf{M_2O_3}\).

(Check: \(\dfrac{2 \times 56}{2 \times 56 + 3 \times 16} \times 100 = \dfrac{112}{160} \times 100 = 70.0\%\), as stated. With At. mass 56, M is iron, and \(\mathrm{M_2O_3}\) is \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}\).)

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed answer is \(\mathrm{FeSO_4}\), which omits the water of crystallisation. The question describes a **hydrated** salt and supplies 0.4532 g of water explicitly, and that mass fixes the hydration exactly: 0.4532/18 = 0.02518 mol of water against 0.2014/56 = 0.003596 mol of iron, a ratio of 7.00. The complete empirical formula of the substance described is \(\mathrm{FeSO_4 \cdot 7H_2O}\). The printed \(\mathrm{FeSO_4}\) is correct for the anhydrous part alone — its own O count is 4.00 — but it does not answer the question as asked.]

The four masses given add to \(0.2014 + 0.1153 + 0.2301 + 0.4532 = 1.0000\ \mathrm{g}\), i.e. the whole sample is accounted for. Note that the 0.2301 g of oxygen is the oxygen of the *salt*; the oxygen of the water of crystallisation is counted inside the 0.4532 g of water. Treat the water as a single unit of formula mass \(18\).

Moles of Fe \(= \dfrac{0.2014}{56} = 0.003596\)

Moles of S \(= \dfrac{0.1153}{32} = 0.003603\)

Moles of O \(= \dfrac{0.2301}{16} = 0.014381\)

Moles of \(\mathrm{H_2O} = \dfrac{0.4532}{18} = 0.025178\)

Divide throughout by the smallest, 0.003596:

Fe \(= 1\), S \(= 1.00\), O \(= 4.00\), \(\mathrm{H_2O} = 7.00\)

So one formula unit holds one Fe, one S, four O and seven waters:

\(\therefore\) the empirical formula of the hydrated salt is \(\mathbf{FeSO_4 \cdot 7H_2O}\) — green vitriol, the same salt as in part F.

The three percentages given total \(20 + 6.7 + 46.67 = 73.37\), which is less than 100, and the stem says the compound contains oxygen. So the oxygen is found by difference:

\(\%\ \mathrm{O} = 100 - 73.37 = 26.63\%\)

Take 100 g and convert to moles:

Moles of C \(= \dfrac{20}{12} = 1.667\)

Moles of H \(= \dfrac{6.7}{1.008} = 6.647\)

Moles of N \(= \dfrac{46.67}{14} = 3.334\)

Moles of O \(= \dfrac{26.63}{16} = 1.664\)

Divide by the smallest, 1.664:

C \(= 1.00\), H \(= 3.99 \approx 4\), N \(= 2.00\), O \(= 1\)

Empirical formula \(= \mathrm{CH_4N_2O}\), whose empirical formula mass is \(12 + 4 + 28 + 16 = 60\).

\(r = \dfrac{\text{Molar mass}}{\text{Empirical formula mass}} = \dfrac{60}{60} = 1\)

\(\therefore\) the molecular formula is \(\mathbf{CH_4N_2O}\), i.e. \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\) — urea, the compound of Problem 2.15.

The percentages total \(9.09 + 36.36 + 54.55 = 100.00\), so nothing has to be found by difference.

Take 100 g and convert to moles:

Moles of C \(= \dfrac{54.55}{12} = 4.546\)

Moles of H \(= \dfrac{9.09}{1.008} = 9.018\)

Moles of O \(= \dfrac{36.36}{16} = 2.273\)

Divide by the smallest, 2.273:

C \(= 2.00\), H \(= 3.97 \approx 4\), O \(= 1\)

Empirical formula \(= \mathrm{C_2H_4O}\); empirical formula mass \(= 24 + 4 + 16 = 44\).

\(r = \dfrac{88}{44} = 2\)

On heating in the absence of air the carbohydrate decomposes into carbon and water only, so the residue is all the carbon the sample contained and the rest of the mass left as water.

Mass of carbon \(= 124\ \mathrm{g}\)

Mass of water \(= 310 - 124 = 186\ \mathrm{g}\)

Convert both to moles (taking \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) as a unit of formula mass 18):

Moles of C \(= \dfrac{124}{12} = 10.333\)

Moles of \(\mathrm{H_2O} = \dfrac{186}{18} = 10.333\)

Dividing by the smaller value gives C : \(\mathrm{H_2O} = 1 : 1\), so one carbon atom accompanies one water unit.

\(\therefore\) the empirical formula is \(\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{H_2O})\), i.e. \(\mathbf{CH_2O}\).

(This is why the class is named *carbo-hydrate*: its empirical formula is carbon combined with water in a 1 : 1 ratio. Note the empirical formula alone cannot say which carbohydrate it is — glucose \(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\) and formaldehyde \(\mathrm{CH_2O}\) share it; the molar mass would be needed to settle that.)

**a. \(3{,}672{,}199 = 3.672199 \times 10^{6}\)** — the decimal point moves 6 places to the left.

**b. \(0.000098 = 9.8 \times 10^{-5}\)** — the decimal point moves 5 places to the right.

**c. \(0.00461 = 4.61 \times 10^{-3}\)** — the decimal point moves 3 places to the right.

**d. \(198.75 = 1.9875 \times 10^{2}\)** — the decimal point moves 2 places to the left.

The exponent gives the number of places to shift the decimal point: to the left for a negative exponent, to the right for a positive one.

**a.** \(3.49 \times 10^{-11} = 0.0000000000349\)

**b.** \(3.75 \times 10^{-1} = 0.375\)

Note that (d), (e) and (g) are not written in *standard* scientific form to begin with — their coefficients do not satisfy \(1 \leqslant N < 10\) — which is exactly why the shift is not simply the exponent's worth of zeros.

For addition and subtraction the exponents are first made equal, then the coefficients are added or subtracted; the result carries as many places as the coarsest term.

**a.** \(3.971 \times 10^7 + 1.98 \times 10^4 = 3.971 \times 10^7 + 0.00198 \times 10^7\)

\(= (3.971 + 0.00198) \times 10^7 = 3.97298 \times 10^7\)

The coarser term, \(3.971 \times 10^7\), is known only to the \(10^4\) place, so

\(\approx \mathbf{3.973 \times 10^{7}}\)

**b.** \(1.05 \times 10^{-4} - 9.7 \times 10^{-5} = 1.05 \times 10^{-4} - 0.97 \times 10^{-4}\)

\(= (1.05 - 0.97) \times 10^{-4} = 0.08 \times 10^{-4} = \mathbf{8 \times 10^{-6}}\)

Both terms are known to the \(10^{-6}\) place, so the difference retains only one significant figure — subtraction of two close numbers costs precision.

The first is not. This chapter defines relative deviation as **mean absolute deviation ÷ mean**, and applies that definition in its own Problem 2.6; here the three masses are 0.7783, 0.7780 and 0.7786 g, the mean is 0.7783 g, the absolute deviations are 0.0000, 0.0003 and 0.0003 g, and the mean absolute deviation is therefore ±0.0002 g — giving a relative deviation of 0.0002/0.7783 × 100 = **0.026 %**, not 0.077 %. Eight candidate routes to the printed 0.07736 % were tested and none reproduces it; the closest is 0.0771 %, obtained by dividing the SUM of the three deviations by the mean instead of their mean, which is itself a departure from the chapter's own definition. So the printed figure cannot be reconstructed exactly, and it is roughly three times the correct relative deviation.]

First get the three masses of acetone by subtracting the mass of the empty bottle, 38.0015 g:

\(38.7798 - 38.0015 = 0.7783\ \mathrm{g}\)

\(38.7795 - 38.0015 = 0.7780\ \mathrm{g}\)

\(38.7801 - 38.0015 = 0.7786\ \mathrm{g}\)

**Precision** — how closely the readings agree among themselves.

Mean \(= \dfrac{0.7783 + 0.7780 + 0.7786}{3} = \dfrac{2.3349}{3} = 0.7783\ \mathrm{g}\)

Absolute deviations \(= |\,\text{Observed} - \text{Mean}\,| = 0.0000,\ 0.0003,\ 0.0003\ \mathrm{g}\)

Mean absolute deviation \(= \dfrac{0.0000 + 0.0003 + 0.0003}{3} = \pm 0.0002\ \mathrm{g}\)

Relative deviation \(= \dfrac{0.0002}{0.7783} \times 100 = \mathbf{0.026\%}\)

**Accuracy** — how close the result is to the true value, 0.7791 g.

Absolute error \(=\) Observed \(-\) True \(= 0.7783 - 0.7791 = -0.0008\ \mathrm{g}\)

Relative error \(= \dfrac{-0.0008}{0.7791} \times 100 = \mathbf{-0.103\%}\)

**Characterisation.** The measurements are highly **precise** — they scatter by only about 0.03 % about their own mean, which is what a balance reading to 0.0001 g should give. They are slightly less **accurate**: the mean is low by 0.0008 g, a relative error of about 0.1 %, roughly four times the scatter. Because the error is larger than the spread and always in the same direction, it is a *systematic* error (a bias — for instance in the recorded mass of the empty bottle) rather than random scatter. This illustrates the chapter's point that high precision is a prerequisite for high accuracy but does not by itself guarantee it.

The metre stick is graduated in millimetres, so its **least count is 1 mm = 0.1 cm**. By the convention this chapter sets out for the burette — a burette of least count 0.1 mL is read as 10.2 mL, the last digit being the single uncertain one — a reading from this stick must be recorded to the 0.1 cm place and no further.

**a. The measurement to accept is 12.6 cm.**

It is quoted to exactly the least count of the instrument: the 12 is certain and the 6 is the one estimated digit, so the reading properly means \(12.6 \pm 0.1\ \mathrm{cm}\). It carries every figure the metre stick can support and none that it cannot.

**b. Reasons for rejecting each of the others**

| Measurement | Reason for rejection |
|---|---|
| 12.65 cm (given twice) | Claims a digit in the 0.01 cm place, one place finer than the least count of 0.1 cm. The stick cannot resolve hundredths of a centimetre, so the final 5 is not a legitimate estimated digit — it overstates the precision. |
| 12.655 cm | Worse still: two digits beyond the least count. Its last figure implies a resolution of 0.001 cm, ten times finer than the instrument can even estimate. |
| 126.55 mm | The same value as 12.655 cm merely re-expressed in millimetres, and rejected for the same reason — changing the unit cannot add precision the instrument never had. |
| 12 cm | The opposite fault: it stops one place short, discarding the 0.1 cm digit that the stick *can* resolve. It throws away real information and understates the precision of the measurement. |

So of the six, one over-reports precision three times over, one under-reports it, and only 12.6 cm states exactly what the instrument can support.

Calcium carbonate decomposes on heating according to the balanced equation

\(\mathrm{CaCO_3} \xrightarrow{\ \Delta\ } \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO_2}\uparrow\)

Write the relative masses below the formulae, using the atomic masses given:

\(\mathrm{CaCO_3} = 40 + 12 + (3 \times 16) = 100\) parts

\(\mathrm{CaO} = 40 + 16 = 56\) parts

So 100 g of calcium carbonate produces 56 g of calcium oxide.

\(\therefore\) 19.3 g of \(\mathrm{CaCO_3}\) will produce

\(= \dfrac{56}{100} \times 19.3 = 10.808\ \mathrm{g}\)

\(\approx \mathbf{10.8\ g\ of\ CaO}\)

(The remaining \(19.3 - 10.8 = 8.5\ \mathrm{g}\) leaves as carbon dioxide, so the mass of the solid residue is less than the mass taken.)

Sucrose is \(\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}}\) and it "burns" in the body by the same balanced equation as combustion:

\(\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}} + 12\,\mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow 12\,\mathrm{CO_2} + 11\,\mathrm{H_2O}\)

**Step 1 — sucrose needed for one day.** 34 g satisfies one hour, so a day of 24 hours requires

\(34 \times 24 = 816\ \mathrm{g}\) of sucrose.

**Step 2 — moles of sucrose.** Molar mass \(= (12 \times 12) + (22 \times 1) + (11 \times 16) = 144 + 22 + 176 = 342\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

Moles \(= \dfrac{816}{342} = 2.386\ \mathrm{mol}\)

**Step 3 — moles of oxygen.** The equation requires 12 mol of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) per mole of sucrose:

\(12 \times 2.386 = 28.632\ \mathrm{mol}\ \mathrm{O_2}\)

**Step 4 — mass of oxygen.** Molar mass of \(\mathrm{O_2} = 32\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\):

\(28.632 \times 32 = \mathbf{916.21\ g\ of\ O_2}\)

So a little over 0.9 kg of oxygen would have to be carried per astronaut per day for this requirement alone.
